newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Albright vows war crimes suspects to face justice.
newsitem.headline: Albright vows war crimes suspects to face justice.

text.p: U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright travelled to the heart of Bosnian Serb territory on Sunday to reassert American determination that indicted war criminals will be brought to justice.
In the northern town of Brcko, where Serb forces remain in control after seizing the area early in the Bosnian war, Albright warned that Washington wanted war crimes suspects to face trial.
"Brcko was the scene of some of the worst violence and brutality of the war," she said. "Make no mistake, a price will be paid for the atrocities that were committed here.
"Until it is paid by those who perpetrated the crimes, it will be paid by those who protected them".
Albright, using blunt language, spent the weekend in the Balkans to press a new U.S. campaign to force compliance with the 1995 Dayton accords that ended the Bosnian conflict.
The U.N. war crimes tribunal in the Hague has indicted 75 people for war crimes, but most of them -- including former Bosnian Serb president Radovan Karadzic -- remain at large.
The United States has explored the possibility of a special military unit to snatch suspects and bring them to the Hague, but so far no action has been taken.
Albright has said repeatedly that Washington is examining "all options".

After visiting U.S. peacekeeping troops stationed in Brcko, she later flew to the northwestern town of Banja Luka, where she was due to meet Biljana Plavsic, president of Bosnia's autonomous Serb republic.

Albright's visit was intended to underscore the U.S. position that it will work only with Bosnian authorities willing to comply with the peace agreement. Her visit to Banja Luka was seen as rebuke to hardline leaders based in Pale, outside Sarajevo, who have tried to undercut Plavsic.
During her stop in Brcko, Albright celebrated the reopening of a bridge that had been closed since war erupted in former Yugoslavia in 1991.
She had urged Croatian President Franjo Tudjman on Saturday to reopen the bridge, and he obliged.
Albright said that Brcko over the years had been an "open gate to the markets of Europe" and that opening the bridge would would restore Bosnia's links to the rest of the continent.
Issuing an appeal for tolerance, she said: "This bridge is both literally and symbolically a road to Europe.
"It leads away from the horrors and hatreds that made so much of this century so tragic for the people of this country.
"If you travel in that direction, you will eventually reach a Europe where borders unite rather than divide, a Europe where reason has triumphed over revenge..."
Albright's visit coincided with growing international concern that the fragile peace is unravelling, only a year before the NATO-led peace force is due to withdraw.

NATO troops have separated rival armies but nationalist authorities are seeking to seal the results of wartime "ethnic cleansing" by discouraging reconciliation and blocking refugees from returning to their homes.
Albright earlier toured the capital Sarajevo and placed flowers on the Vrbanja bridge to mourn the war's first victim, Suada Dilberovic, who was cut down by sniper fire during a 1992 demonstration.
She chatted with children at a playground and took a stroll down the notorious former "Sniper's Alley" where Sarajevans once dashed across intersections during the nationalist Serb siege of the city.

Albright flew to Bosnia a day after delivering stern warnings to leaders of Bosnia's powerful neighbours, Croatia and Serbia, who sought to carve up the country between them during the 1992-95 conflict.

Using blunt language, Albright reprimanded presidents Franjo Tudjman of Croatia and Slobodan Milosevic of Serbia for failing to hand over indicted war criminals and dragging their feet on other key aspects of the U.S.-brokered peace agreement.
In the Croatian capital Zagreb, Albright said she told Tudjman that he must prevent violence against minority Serb war refugees trying to return to Croatia.
